# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why2: The question and two named choices are clear on first reading, and although the hint is long, it says plainly what happens and that it costs 400 credits.
screens.why3: I can pick the voice I prefer, but my people are deaf or hard of hearing, so what matters is whether they can read the face and the on-screen words, and a voice sample can't show me that.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct and the samples are useful, but they differ only by voice, with no look at the face or lip-readability and no written-only link, which is the choice I'd most want for this audience.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and acknowledges they may read and type instead of listening, so nothing I typed has changed.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Every question is written on screen, and people can type or tap their answers. Options: Daphne (see and hear a 5 s sample with captions) / Saskia (see and hear a 5 s sample with captions) / No interviewer: written questions only.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people will answer, the last step before sending is obviously who receives the link.
screens.why2: The question and all three options are plain to me on first reading; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page and its name says what it is.
screens.why3: I know how I would reach deaf and hard-of-hearing people: those I know by name, a list I search for, or a community group where they already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, each says plainly how the link gets out, and no escape chip is needed because the three cover the choice.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed here, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as sending each their own link.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits under the title, and each card ties it to its deciding number (7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7), with the worst-of-all-cards rule stated.
screens.why_b2: This page draws no chart, but each card's line says what is counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word, even though the statement above them is garbled.
screens.why_b4: The page says my three beliefs held but never what that means for the idea or what to do next, and it doesn't even point me to the 3 people who set a condition on wearing the glasses.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but a clean 7 of 7, "7 of them a lot", is shown without saying that seven is a small group or that it only speaks for those who answered.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 people, a small group: all 7 say the glasses would have helped, so the solution isn't what to worry about, and next I should read the 3 conditions on wearing them; and fix the statement to: while people nearby talk, the wearer sees live captions of what they say inside the lens.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits directly beside 7 of 7 and the bar of 5 of 7, so I can see that the count decides the verdict and clears the bar.
screens.why_b2: Yes 4, with some steps 3 and no 0 add up to the seven people counted, and the strip shows all seven past the marker at 5, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The name Compatibility and the line about their phone being with them and online are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me the phone is not the obstacle and sends me to Adoption friction, which is where I should look next.
screens.why_b5: The count line says a small group is a lean, not a call, and n stays visible, but the So line flatly says the phone is not what will stop them and that Adoption friction is, while the three 'with some steps' answers come with comments about trials and hall pickup that don't say what stood between them and a phone that was with them and online.
screens.instead: So: all 7 had their phone with them and online last time, 3 with some steps, so among these few the phone doesn't look like the obstacle; Adoption friction, below, looks like the bigger risk.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "7 of 7 said it would have gone better, 7 of them a lot · bar 5 of 7", so I have the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see it counts people who said better, over 7, all of them "a lot", with my bar at 5 of 7; "Better · 7 7 a lot" is a bit terse but needs no second read.
screens.why_b3: The card's name and belief line are the ones I checked, down to "following more without asking anyone to repeat".
screens.why_b4: The So line says they only imagined it and points me to Adoption friction, which tells me where to read next but not what this result means for the idea or what to do about it.
screens.why_b5: The small group and the hypothetical are both said, but "Holding up" sits on my belief about following more without asking anyone to repeat, while the question only asked whether the conversation would have gone better, so the benefit itself is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: All 7 imagined their last conversation going a lot better, but that's a lean from a small group, and they were asked about "better", not about following more without asking anyone to repeat; so don't lean on this as proof of the benefit: ask people who have worn the glasses what actually changed, and check Adoption friction below to see if they would wear them.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 3 on a condition", so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each answer to whether they'd wear the glasses, the four rows add up to 7 with for and against marked, and the bar is plain at 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone" are the name and belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line points me to what would make it worth it to the 3, but the only thing below is Tomás's remark about taking the end seat, which doesn't answer that, so I still don't know what to do about those 3.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called a lean and the 3 conditional answers are shown apart, but the So line promises reasons from those 3 that the screen doesn't deliver, and "7 of 7 would do it" reads firmer than 4 unconditional yeses.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is and 3 only if clearly worth it; none of the 3 said what would make it worth it, though Tomás already manages by taking the end seat, so ask those 3 what would have to be true before treating this as settled.

screens.why_b1: Each box states its verdict (Holding up, Compatibility held) with the deciding number beside it: 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines, phone with them and online and wear the glasses paired to the phone, are the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The only framing is the generic 'held, 7 of 7; what they added', so I have to work out for myself that people want to try a pair in their own hard setting first, and that the mic range and one-sided hearing are open questions.
screens.why_b5: The counts are visible and the 2 who never saw the question are named, but 7 of 7 is never called a small group, and the phone belief reads as cleanly held while the three quotes shown are about trialling the glasses or the audio pickup, not the phone.
screens.why_b6: I did not type any of this: a demo on a noisy walk, reading the lens under stage lights, catching audience questions in a big hall, and a one-side-deaf person's end-seat workaround that competes with the glasses.
screens.instead: Say: 'Held, but only 7 people answered; before ordering, two want to try a pair in their own hard setting, one wants it to catch audience questions, and one gets by taking the end seat, so offer a real-setting trial and test mic range and one-sided hearing next.'

screens.why1: As the first thing asked of me, checking that I regularly talk with hearing people is an obvious way to see whether this study is meant for me.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is exactly how I would say it, and I can answer on first reading, though "talk" could make a person who signs through an interpreter pause for a moment.
screens.why3: I know whether I talked with hearing people this week because it is part of my ordinary life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover the question cleanly, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, company or plan reaches me, and "hearing people" is my own community's term.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two simple options, although "I'll read 2 options" is slightly more than a yes-or-no needs.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost the thread of one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I'd say it myself and "lose track of a conversation" is what happens to me, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people in the last week, because it's part of my ordinary life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but two escape chips is one too many, and "I can't recall one particular conversation" is a long, odd fit for a question that doesn't ask me to pick one.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company reaches me, only a plain question about my week in words I use.
screens.why6: It's one short question with "Yes or no" at the end, so I could take it in once and answer, and no spoken escape is right for a gate.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes / No (one chip only: I can't recall)

screens.why1: After being asked whether I lost track of a conversation, and with the screen marked as an idea to consider, it is obvious why I am being shown captions for that problem.
screens.why2: Live captions are everyday words for me, and glasses, app and lens are plain, so I get it on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: It is about the conversations I have with hearing people and the lipreading and eye contact I already juggle, so I can picture it in my own life.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose under Imagine, and it speaks to me as someone wearing the glasses, with no internal terms or roles for people leaking through.
screens.why6: It says well in short sentences with no symbols or parentheses, but five sentences is a lot to hold at one hearing, and the how repeats that captions appear in the glasses before the belief line comes.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, it makes sense to ask whether I had what they would need, though the screen doesn't say the phone is what the glasses rely on.
screens.why2: "Have your phone with you and online?" is a clipped fragment with no subject, and "last conversation" doesn't say with hearing people, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know whether my phone was on me and had signal at my last conversation.
screens.why4: Yes, No and I can't tell are clear, but "Yes, with some steps" is odd for a phone that either was with me and online or wasn't, though I could stretch it to mean digging it out or turning on data.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose and nothing else of the product or its makers' terms reaches me, with the phone asked about only as a plain fact of my day.
screens.why6: It is short and the three options hold easily, but the clipped "Have your phone with you and online?" sounds like a broken sentence when heard once, with "some steps" unclear.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Did you have your phone with you and online? Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: It makes sense as a follow-up if I said getting my phone out and online took some steps, but it comes abruptly and doesn't say which steps it means.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but I have to read it twice to work out that "it" means having my phone with me and online.
screens.why3: I know what I had to do to have my phone ready in that conversation, such as finding it, unlocking it or getting a signal.
screens.why4: The screen shows only a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product, the company's plans or the founder's terms for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says easily and can be answered after one hearing, though the "it" relies on my remembering the question before.
screens.instead: What did you have to do to have your phone with you and online in that conversation?

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the steps I would need, it is obvious why they ask whether the glasses would have helped in that conversation.
screens.why2: I can follow this on first reading and answer it straight away, because going better or not is how I would talk about a conversation myself.
screens.why3: I was in that conversation and know where I lost track, so I can judge whether captions in front of my eyes would have helped, though I have not tried them.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every answer without overlap, and I can't tell fits someone who has never worn captioning glasses.
screens.why5: The product name and live captions come only from the idea card shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options that are easy to hold when read as a list and one escape said last, though on this link I would be relying on the screen or captions as much as the voice.

screens.why1: After being shown the glasses and asked if they would have helped, it makes obvious sense to ask whether I would actually wear them.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone is plain and I can answer it on first reading, since I already pair hearing devices and apps with a phone.
screens.why3: Whether I would put on captioning glasses in a conversation is my own decision, drawn from how I already manage hearing people, devices and being seen using them.
screens.why4: The options cover the range and the escape fits, but 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' overlaps with 'Probably not' for someone unsure, and I would hesitate over which one is mine.
screens.why5: The idea card shows the name and the glasses on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is short, one question with a set-up clause, four short options I can hold and one escape said last.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I'd wear the glasses and whether they'd have helped my last conversation, it makes sense to ask what would make them worth it to me.
screens.why2: Short everyday words I can take in on first reading or hearing, and the name AirCaps comes from the idea card I was just shown.
screens.why3: I can say what I'd need from captions in a noisy room or a theatre, such as accuracy and keeping up with speech, but I haven't used the glasses so part of my answer is a guess, and 'worth it' leaves open whether that means money or hassle.
screens.why4: It is only a box to type in, with no options, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The product name was shown to me on purpose on the idea card, and nothing new about the founder's plans or terms for people reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says easily in one breath, and I could answer it the first time I heard it, though typing or speaking is my choice as a deaf person.
